data.name: AccAccountsTreeTitle
data.value: Chart of Accounts

data.name: AccAccountsTreeWhat
data.value: The chart of accounts is the structure in which your organization's accounts are arranged into groups and sub-accounts. It is the foundation of every accounting operation in the system; no journal entry can be posted without referencing an account defined in the chart. Accounts are usually classified into assets, liabilities, equity, revenue, and expenses, and the system uses a structured code scheme to organize each account under its parent.

data.name: AccAccountsTreeHow
data.value:
1. Open the Accounting menu and choose Chart of Accounts.
2. Accounts appear as a tree; expand any group by clicking the arrow next to its name.
3. To add an account, click Add, then choose the parent account the new account will belong to.
4. Enter the code and the Arabic name (English name is optional), set the appropriate account type, and save.
We recommend planning the chart carefully before recording transactions, because main accounts are usually created once and then detailed accounts are added underneath them.

data.name: AccAccountsTreeConcept
data.value: Every account in the chart has a debit or credit nature: a debit account is one that increases on the debit side of an entry, and a credit account increases on the credit side. This classification is a mathematical rule that keeps the system balanced (total debits always equal total credits); it is not a judgment about whether an account is beneficial or not.

data.name: AccJournalEntriesTitle
data.value: Journal Entries

data.name: AccJournalEntriesWhat
data.value: The journal is the detailed record of every accounting operation the organization records, from invoices and returns to cash transfers and adjustments. Each entry shows the transaction date, description, the debited and credited accounts, and the amounts, and is recorded on at least two lines according to the double-entry rule.

data.name: AccJournalEntriesHow
data.value:
1. Open the Accounting menu and choose Journal Entries.
2. Click Add Entry, set the date, then write the entry description.
3. Add lines one by one: for each line pick the account from the chart, enter the amount, and mark the side as debit or credit.
4. Make sure the debit and credit totals are equal; the system will not accept an unbalanced entry.
5. Review the displayed entry and save.

data.name: AccGeneralLedgerTitle
data.value: General Ledger

data.name: AccGeneralLedgerWhat
data.value: The general ledger shows the movement of a single account over time. It gathers every entry that touches that account, orders them by date, and shows the running balance after each movement. This is the report you consult when you ask how much a certain account stands at and why.

data.name: AccGeneralLedgerHow
data.value:
1. Open the General Ledger report from the Reports menu, or from the chart of accounts page itself.
2. Select the account and set the date range (from and to).
3. Click View to see a table with each movement's date, entry number, description, debit and credit values, and the balance after the movement.
4. You can print or export the report using the report action buttons.

data.name: AccGeneralLedgerConcept
data.value: The balance shown in the ledger is cumulative: opening balance plus additions minus reductions equals the closing balance. Any break in this equation usually points to an earlier incomplete entry, which makes the ledger the first place to check.

data.name: AccTrialBalanceTitle
data.value: Trial Balance

data.name: AccTrialBalanceWhat
data.value: The trial balance is a listing of all accounts and their balances at a given date, split into debit and credit sides. Its purpose is to verify that recorded entries are balanced, and it is the starting point before preparing the financial statements.

data.name: AccTrialBalanceHow
data.value:
1. Open the Trial Balance report from the Reports menu.
2. Set the period or the ending date, then click Generate Report.
3. Review the table: the total debit side must equal the total credit side.
4. If a difference appears, it indicates a missing or mis-recorded entry, so review the journal before relying on any financial statement.

data.name: AccTrialBalanceConcept
data.value: An even trial balance is only a mathematical check, not proof that the operations are economically correct; two errors of equal amount can cancel out. That is why physical stock counts and invoice reviews remain necessary, and why the trial balance alone is not enough to certify the books.

data.name: AccFinancialStatementsTitle
data.value: Financial Statements

data.name: AccFinancialStatementsWhat
data.value: Financial statements are the final product of the accounting cycle. The most important are the balance sheet, which shows assets, liabilities, and equity at a given date, and the income statement, which shows revenues, expenses, and net profit for a period. The system builds both statements automatically from the recorded journal entries.

data.name: AccFinancialStatementsHow
data.value:
1. Open the Financial Statements report from the Reports menu.
2. Choose the statement type (balance sheet or income statement), set the period, and click Generate.
3. Review the figures, then print or export the report.
4. Before relying on them, make sure the journal is complete and the trial balance matches.

data.name: InvItemsTitle
data.value: Items

data.name: InvItemsWhat
data.value: Items are the trading units your organization sells or purchases. Each item has a unique code, Arabic and English names, a category, a unit of measure, a cost price, a sale price, minimum and maximum stock levels, and may carry a barcode or an image that appears on the POS buttons.

data.name: InvItemsHow
data.value:
1. Open the Inventory menu and choose Items.
2. Click Add Item, then enter the code and both names (Arabic and English).
3. Select the category and unit, and enter cost price, sale price, and the minimum and maximum stock levels.
4. If the item has a barcode, enter it so it can be scanned at the POS and during receiving; you can also attach an image.
5. Save; to change prices later, open the item, and deactivate instead of deleting items that have transaction history.

data.name: InvItemsConcept
data.value: The cost price is the basis on which inventory balances are valued and profit margins are calculated in reports, while the sale price is what invoices and the POS rely on. Any change to the cost affects inventory value and later profits, so keep it accurate.

data.name: InvCategoriesTitle
data.value: Categories

data.name: InvCategoriesWhat
data.value: Categories are an organizational tool that groups similar items together, such as meat, dairy, or medicine. They are used for filtering and search, for inventory-by-category reports, and for organizing the POS item grid.

data.name: InvCategoriesHow
data.value:
1. Open the Inventory menu and choose Categories.
2. Click Add Category, enter the Arabic name (English is optional), and save.
3. Rename or edit a category from its row in the list whenever needed.
4. Do not delete a category that still has items assigned; reclassify the items first.

data.name: InvCategoriesConcept
data.value: A category is a descriptive field for classification and analysis only; it does not directly move any account. But consistent categorization is what makes item profitability and inventory distribution reports meaningful, because it is the lens through which product groups are read.

data.name: InvUnitsTitle
data.value: Units of Measure

data.name: InvUnitsWhat
data.value: A unit of measure is the way quantities are sold or bought, such as pack, piece, kilogram, or liter. Each item is tied to a single unit that keeps quantity recording consistent across inventory movements, invoices, and the POS.

data.name: InvUnitsHow
data.value:
1. Open the Inventory menu and choose Units.
2. Click Add Unit, enter its name, and save.
3. Assign each item its unit from the item page itself.
4. If your business deals in fractional quantities (such as 1.5 kg), make sure decimals are entered in the allowed fields.

data.name: InvWarehousesTitle
data.value: Warehouses

data.name: InvWarehousesWhat
data.value: A warehouse is the physical place where items are stored, such as the main warehouse or a branch store. Stock balances are kept per warehouse, and each warehouse's inbound and outbound movements are recorded separately.

data.name: InvWarehousesHow
data.value:
1. Open the Inventory menu and choose Warehouses.
2. Click Add Warehouse, enter the code and name, and the location if any.
3. Set one warehouse as the default so it is used automatically when invoices are created.
4. When you open an item you will see its balance broken down by warehouse, so you always know where each quantity is.

data.name: InvWarehousesConcept
data.value: Balances are separate per warehouse; a balance never moves from one warehouse to another by itself. Any transfer must be recorded as an inter-warehouse movement so location-level balances stay accurate and each site's numbers match reality.

data.name: InvMovementsTitle
data.value: Inventory Movements

data.name: InvMovementsWhat
data.value: An inventory movement is any change in item quantities, in or out: purchase receipts, sales issues, sales returns, purchase returns, opening balance, adjustment additions or reductions, or transfers between warehouses. Each movement is recorded with its type and reference so the audit trail stays complete.

data.name: InvMovementsHow
data.value:
1. Open the Inventory menu and choose Movements.
2. Click Add Movement, choose the type (in or out), the item, the warehouse, and the quantity.
3. Enter the reference number (invoice or purchase order) if any, then save.
4. The movement updates the item and warehouse balances immediately and appears in the movement log.
5. To move stock between locations, use the Transfer Between Warehouses button and set the source and destination warehouses.

data.name: InvMovementsConcept
data.value: Every stock movement has a matching accounting effect: a sale reduces stock and posts the cost of goods sold, a purchase increases it and posts in the journal. Movements should therefore run through invoices and authorized movement screens, not as a parallel recording path, so inventory figures never drift away from the financial statements.

data.name: InvBatchesTitle
data.value: Batches and Expiry Dates

data.name: InvBatchesWhat
data.value: Batch tracking lets you record each batch of an item with its quantity, production date, and expiry date. It is essential for perishables such as medicine and dairy. The system follows a first-expiry-first-out rule so that soonest-expiring goods are sold first and expired stock does not pile up.

data.name: InvBatchesHow
data.value:
1. Record every batch with its data when receiving goods or through the batch movement screen.
2. At the POS, a near-expiry warning appears on items whose shelf life is coming to an end, so the cashier avoids them or sells them first.
3. Follow the expiry tracking and expiring batches screens from the Inventory menu to set selling or disposal priorities.
4. When a batch expires unsold, record it as a write-off so it leaves the balances officially.

data.name: SalInvoicesTitle
data.value: Sales Invoices

data.name: SalInvoicesWhat
data.value: A sales invoice is the document that records the sale of goods or services to a customer. Recording it reduces the stock of the sold items and posts a journal entry that reflects the revenue, tax, and either the amount owed by the customer or the cash received.

data.name: SalInvoicesHow
data.value:
1. Open the Sales menu and choose Invoices.
2. Click Add Invoice, choose the customer (or a cash customer for over-the-counter sales), and set the date.
3. Add the lines: select the item and its quantity, and make sure the quantity does not exceed available stock.
4. Choose the payment method (cash, card, on account, or check), then save.
5. View and print the invoice; its effect on stock and journal entries appears immediately.

data.name: SalInvoicesConcept
data.value: A sales invoice usually creates two linked entries: one that transfers the cost of the sold goods from inventory to cost of goods sold, and another that records the counterpart (cash, card, or receivables) together with revenue and tax. A credit sale creates a receivable from the customer, while a cash sale is posted to the fund immediately.

data.name: SalReturnsTitle
data.value: Sales Returns

data.name: SalReturnsWhat
data.value: A sales return is a document that reverses a sales invoice, in full or in part, when a customer gives goods back. Recording it returns the goods to stock when they are still sellable and posts a reversing entry that undoes the original invoice's effect.

data.name: SalReturnsHow
data.value:
1. Open the Sales menu and choose Returns.
2. Click Add Return, then search for and select the original invoice; its lines are displayed.
3. Set the quantity to return for each line (full or partial).
4. Choose how the refund will be handled (cash for the full amount, or a reduction of the customer's balance), then save.
5. Review the returned invoice and print if needed.

data.name: SalReturnsConcept
data.value: The purpose of a return is to remove the sale's effect from the statements, not just adjust a number: goods come back to stock, revenue decreases, and the refund is posted either to the fund if cash was returned or as a credit against the customer's balance. A quantity larger than what was sold on the invoice is never accepted.

data.name: SalCustomersTitle
data.value: Customers

data.name: SalCustomersWhat
data.value: The customer register holds the parties the organization sells to, with their names, codes, and credit limits. Credit invoices are addressed from it, and aging reports and statements are built on it.

data.name: SalCustomersHow
data.value:
1. Open the Sales menu and choose Customers.
2. Click Add Customer, enter the code and the Arabic name (English is optional).
3. Set the credit limit if the customer has an on-account relationship.
4. Open a customer page to view their statement and follow up on outstanding amounts.
5. Deactivate rather than delete a customer you no longer deal with if they have history.

data.name: SalCustomersConcept
data.value: The credit limit is a ceiling on the debt an on-account customer may accumulate; it is a risk-control tool, not an accounting constraint. A customer's current balance equals their unpaid invoices, and the statement gathers invoices, receipts, and returns into one place.

data.name: SalQuotesTitle
data.value: Price Quotes

data.name: SalQuotesWhat
data.value: A quote is a preliminary document sent to a customer before the sale is completed, specifying items, quantities, and prices. It moves no stock and posts no entries; it is converted into a sales invoice when the customer accepts it.

data.name: SalQuotesHow
data.value:
1. Open the Sales menu and choose Quotes.
2. Click Add Quote, select the customer, and add the lines and prices.
3. Set a validity date if you use one, then save.
4. When the customer accepts, click the Convert to Invoice action on the quote and a sales invoice will be generated pre-filled with the same lines; complete the usual sales steps from there.

data.name: PurInvoicesTitle
data.value: Purchase Invoices

data.name: PurInvoicesWhat
data.value: A purchase invoice documents the purchase of goods from a supplier. Recording it raises item balances in the receiving warehouse and posts an entry that records the amount owed to the supplier or the cash paid, plus the cost of the goods.

data.name: PurInvoicesHow
data.value:
1. Open the Purchases menu and choose Invoices.
2. Click Add Invoice, then choose the supplier, the receiving warehouse, and the date.
3. Add the lines: item, unit cost, and quantity.
4. At the end, decide whether the invoice is on account (posted to supplier payables) or paid in cash (posted to the fund), then save.
5. You can also convert an accepted purchase order into a receiving invoice using the convert action; then review and print.

data.name: PurInvoicesConcept
data.value: Purchase invoices are the main source of stock increases along with receiving. The entered unit cost is what the balances are valued at, so enter a correct cost that includes any freight or customs charges added to the unit per company policy, because it carries into the profitability reports later.

data.name: PurReturnsTitle
data.value: Purchase Returns

data.name: PurReturnsWhat
data.value: A purchase return reverses a purchase invoice, in full or in part, and is used when goods are sent back to the supplier due to defect, error, or over-delivery. Recording it removes the returned items from stock and posts a reversing entry for the invoice's effect.

data.name: PurReturnsHow
data.value:
1. Open the Purchases menu and choose Returns.
2. Click Add Return and select the original purchase invoice; its lines are displayed.
3. Set the lines and quantities to return.
4. Choose whether the amount will come back in cash or be deducted from the supplier's account, then save.
5. Make sure the returned goods are still fully in stock before recording.

data.name: PurReturnsConcept
data.value: A purchase return reverses the whole movement: stock decreases, supplier balances are reduced, or paid cash comes back. Recording it as a manual stock movement without a return invoice is a mistake, because the financial effect would disappear from the statements and be hard to reconcile later.

data.name: PurSuppliersTitle
data.value: Suppliers

data.name: PurSuppliersWhat
data.value: The supplier register holds the parties the organization buys from, with their names and codes. Purchase invoices are documented against it, and payables aging and supplier statements are built on it.

data.name: PurSuppliersHow
data.value:
1. Open the Purchases menu and choose Suppliers.
2. Click Add Supplier, enter the code and name, then save.
3. Open a supplier page to view their statement and reconcile invoices and payments.
4. Deactivate rather than delete a supplier you no longer work with if they have history.

data.name: PurSuppliersConcept
data.value: A supplier's current balance (what is owed to them) equals their unpaid purchase invoices minus payments and returns. The supplier statement gathers all of these into a single document that settles any dispute over an amount due.

data.name: PurBarcodeReceivingTitle
data.value: Barcode Receiving

data.name: PurBarcodeReceivingWhat
data.value: When receiving purchased goods you can speed up line entry by scanning barcodes directly instead of searching for each item and typing its quantity, which is especially useful for invoices with many lines.

data.name: PurBarcodeReceivingHow
data.value:
1. On the new purchase invoice screen, click the barcode receiving toggle; a field labeled Scan barcode appears.
2. Scan the items one after another and the lines are added automatically.
3. Scan the same item more than once to increase the added quantity.
4. Save the invoice normally when the lines are complete.
5. If a code is not recognized, a message appears to identify the unknown item so you can handle it manually.

data.name: PosSellingTitle
data.value: Cash and Card Sales

data.name: PosSellingWhat
data.value: The point-of-sale screen is designed for fast checkout in front of the customer: you add items with a click or a barcode scan, take the payment, and issue the invoice and receipt within seconds. It supports cash, card, and on-account payment.

data.name: PosSellingHow
data.value:
1. Open the POS from the top navigation or go straight to the POS screen.
2. Add items by clicking their buttons or scanning barcodes in the search field; they accumulate in the cart.
3. Choose the payment method: cash (enter the amount received to see the change) or card (enter the approval code from the terminal receipt and the last four digits).
4. Press Complete Sale to issue the invoice and print the receipt automatically.
Note: you must open a shift before the first sale of the day; otherwise the system will ask you to start one first.

data.name: PosSellingConcept
data.value: A cash invoice posts cash to the fund and transfers the cost of goods; a card invoice posts to the payment-method account with its details. The shift system later compares what was actually sold against the cash found in the drawer, exposing any shortage or surplus before the next shift starts.

data.name: PosReturnsTitle
data.value: Returns at the POS

data.name: PosReturnsWhat
data.value: The POS can return goods that were documented on an earlier sales invoice and refund the customer on the spot, in full or in part. The return works against the original invoice lines to determine the quantities that can still be returned.

data.name: PosReturnsHow
data.value:
1. On the POS screen press the Return button (F6).
2. Search for the original invoice by number or by scanning one of its item barcodes; its lines are shown.
3. Set the quantity to return for each line.
4. Choose the return method: cash from the cash drawer, or against the account if applicable, then save.
5. The return is posted and the goods are added back to stock according to their condition.

data.name: PosReturnsConcept
data.value: You cannot return more than the quantity sold on the invoice, and a damaged item is rejected if policy does not allow it. Accounting-wise the return reverses the sale entry: revenue decreases, cost of returned goods increases, and the refunded cash leaves the drawer.

data.name: PosCashTransferTitle
data.value: Cash Transfers Between Chest and Drawer

data.name: PosCashTransferWhat
data.value: Under the shift system, the cash in the drawer is expected to consist only of the opening float and sales transactions. In the middle of a shift you may need to add more change or withdraw surplus revenue to the main chest; the cash transfer documents these two movements between the cash drawer and the chest.

data.name: PosCashTransferHow
data.value:
1. On the POS screen press the Cash Transfer button (F7).
2. Choose the direction: Float In (from chest) to add extra change, or Cash Out (to chest) to withdraw surplus.
3. Enter the amount and a note, then execute the transfer.
4. The system records the operation and posts an entry between the drawer and chest accounts.
5. Review the movements later in the cash transfer log available from the POS reports.

data.name: PosShortcutsTitle
data.value: Keyboard Shortcuts

data.name: PosShortcutsWhat
data.value: The POS screen supports the F1 to F7 keys to run daily operations quickly without touching the screen. Each key triggers the exact same action as its matching on-screen button, and obeys the same enable/disable conditions.

data.name: PosShortcutsHow
data.value:
1. F1 New invoice (clears the cart and starts a new transaction).
2. F2 Complete sale (issues the invoice with the selected payment method).
3. F3 Select cash payment.
4. F4 Select card payment.
5. F5 Hold the sale (suspend the cart to resume later).
6. F6 Open the return window.
7. F7 Open the cash transfer window.
The keys follow the buttons' own rules: you cannot complete a sale from an empty cart no matter which key you press.

data.name: PosShortcutsConcept
data.value: The shortcuts do not open a parallel path for actions; they call the same functions the buttons call, so all guards remain in force and no rule can be bypassed with a keystroke. They also do not interfere with barcode scanning, since each works in its own lane.

data.name: PosShiftTitle
data.value: Opening and Closing Shifts, Cash Count

data.name: PosShiftWhat
data.value: A shift is a single cashier work period between opening and closing. A shift must be opened with an opening float before the first sale; at the end it is closed by entering what was actually found in the drawer, the difference is calculated and posted if any. This is the backbone of cash control.

data.name: PosShiftHow
data.value:
1. Opening: from the Sales menu choose Start Shift, enter the opening float, then press Start Shift.
2. Closing: choose End Shift and Settle, and the screen shows cash sales, refunds, and transfers.
3. Expected cash equals the opening float plus cash sales minus cash refunds and withdrawals plus additions.
4. Enter the amount counted in the drawer and the system computes the variance (counted minus expected).
5. If the variance is zero the shift balances; otherwise a cash-difference entry is posted automatically. Review the result and confirm the close.
6. The shifts history page (for managers) shows all shifts and their results.

data.name: ChkRegisterTitle
data.value: Recording Incoming and Outgoing Checks

data.name: ChkRegisterWhat
data.value: The bank checks module documents the checks your organization receives from customers (incoming) and the ones it issues to suppliers (outgoing), with the check number, bank, branch, party, amount, and both the issue and due dates.

data.name: ChkRegisterHow
data.value:
1. Open the Reports menu and choose Bank Checks.
2. Click Register New Check.
3. Set the direction: Received from Customer for an incoming check, or Issued to Supplier for an outgoing one.
4. Enter the check number, bank, branch, party (customer or supplier), amount, issue date, and due date.
5. Link the check to its related invoice if there is one, then save; the check appears with the status Registered (awaiting due date).

data.name: ChkRegisterConcept
data.value: Between the issue date and the due date a check remains a pending receivable or payable, not available liquidity. Expected future cash flow is computed from uncollected checks, so registering each check with its correct date is what makes the cash forecast reliable.

data.name: ChkCollectionTitle
data.value: Collection

data.name: ChkCollectionWhat
data.value: Collecting a check means actually cashing its value at the bank or transferring it to the organization's account. Moving a check from the registered state to collected means its value has become available liquidity.

data.name: ChkCollectionHow
data.value:
1. From the checks list choose the incoming check you want.
2. Click the Deposit for Collection action (available for received checks only) when handing it to the bank.
3. When the value arrives, click the Collect Check action.
4. Set the operation date and add a note if needed, then save.
5. On collection, an entry is posted that moves the amount from the outstanding checks account to the fund or the bank account.

data.name: ChkCollectionConcept
data.value: The difference between a registered and a collected check: a registered one is a pending amount waiting for its due date, while a collected one is available cash that can be spent. That is why the financial statements do not count uncollected checks as available liquidity.

data.name: ChkBounceTitle
data.value: Bouncing

data.name: ChkBounceWhat
data.value: A bounced check is one the bank refuses to pay, because of insufficient funds, a mismatched signature, or another reason. The system records the bounce so the check returns to a state that allows follow-up with the party concerned.

data.name: ChkBounceHow
data.value:
1. From the checks list choose the bounced check.
2. Click the Bounce Check action, set the date, and write a note about the reason, then save.
3. The check changes to the Bounced status and appears in the report under overdue checks that need follow-up.
4. Once resolved with the party, you can deposit it for collection again if its state allows it.

data.name: ChkBounceConcept
data.value: A bounce is a sign of deteriorating receivable quality: value that was treated as available liquidity turns back into a doubtful, then problematic, receivable. Recording the bounce in time keeps the aging report accurate and directs follow-up toward the checks most at risk of loss.

data.name: ChkDueDatesTitle
data.value: Due Date Report

data.name: ChkDueDatesWhat
data.value: The checks report displays checks by due date and direction, with a prominent section for overdue checks that need follow-up and a monthly forecast of the expected cash flow from checks.

data.name: ChkDueDatesHow
data.value:
1. Open the Checks Report from the Reports menu segment.
2. Filter by direction (incoming/outgoing/all) and by status, then view.
3. Read the Due to Us (incoming) and Due from Us (outgoing) sections and the net expected flow for each month.
4. Review the overdue checks section and prioritize follow-up with the banks and the two parties.
5. Print or export the report for periodic distribution.

data.name: HrDepartmentsTitle
data.value: Departments

data.name: HrDepartmentsWhat
data.value: Departments are the first building block of the organizational structure, such as sales or accounts, and can have sub-departments under a parent. Positions and employees are classified by department for organization and reporting.

data.name: HrDepartmentsHow
data.value:
1. Open the Human Resources menu and choose Departments.
2. Click Add Department, enter the department code (for example HR) and the Arabic name (English is optional).
3. Select the parent department if any, then save.
4. Non-system departments can be edited and deleted as long as they are not linked to employees.

data.name: HrDepartmentsConcept
data.value: A department is an organizational field; it does not set up an accounting account directly, but using it consistently makes employee reports and permission roles clearer and reduces confusion when assigning tasks and responsibilities.

data.name: HrPositionsTitle
data.value: Job Positions

data.name: HrPositionsWhat
data.value: A position defines the nature of an employee's work inside a department, such as accountant or pharmacist, and is tied to a code and Arabic and English names. It can be activated or deactivated as the organization needs.

data.name: HrPositionsHow
data.value: 1. Open the Human Resources menu and choose Positions.\n2. Click Add Position, enter the code (for example ACC-MGR) and the Arabic and English names, then save.\n3. Deactivate rather than delete positions that are no longer used if they are linked to employees.

data.name: HrPositionsConcept
data.value: Keeping departments and positions separate allows the same position to exist in more than one department and multiple positions in one department, keeping the employee structure flexible against the reality of work instead of a rigid single-level classification.

data.name: HrEmployeesTitle
data.value: Employees

data.name: HrEmployeesWhat
data.value: The employee register holds the data of the people who work in the organization and links each one to a department and a position, making it the main reference for workforce data and the basis for handling leaves and payroll.

data.name: HrEmployeesHow
data.value:
1. Open the Human Resources menu and choose Employees.
2. Click Add Employee, enter the name and basic details, then choose the department and position.
3. Save, then open any employee to view their details and leave history.
4. When an employee leaves, deactivate instead of deleting so the system keeps their previous history intact.

data.name: HrEmployeesConcept
data.value: The administrative employee file is separate from the system login account: an employee may exist without a login, and a cashier may have a login without being in the employee register. The two files are linked from the users screen when needed.

data.name: HrLeavesTitle
data.value: Leaves

data.name: HrLeavesWhat
data.value: The leaves module records employee leaves by type (annual, sick, unpaid) with their duration and reason, so attendance follow-up and absence control can be built on them later.

data.name: HrLeavesHow
data.value:
1. Open the Human Resources menu and choose Leaves.
2. Click Add Leave, choose the employee, the leave type, and the start and end dates.
3. Add a note if needed, then save.
4. Filter the log by page, employee, or period to review each employee's record.

data.name: RepRatiosTitle
data.value: Financial Ratios

data.name: RepRatiosWhat
data.value: The financial ratios report turns statement figures into comparable indicators such as liquidity, profitability, and efficiency, letting a manager read the health of the organization at a glance instead of scanning long tables.

data.name: RepRatiosHow
data.value:
1. Open the Reports menu and choose Financial Ratios.
2. Set the period and click Generate Report.
3. Read the displayed ratios and compare the current period with the previous one where the system offers it.
4. Export or print the report for review meetings.

data.name: RepRatiosConcept
data.value: Ratios are indicators, not verdicts: a rising margin is relative, so the real judgment comes from comparing it with the previous period and with activity volume. Ratios expose problems such as eroding margins or tight liquidity early and push you into the details before they grow.

data.name: RepAgingTitle
data.value: Aging of Receivables and Payables

data.name: RepAgingWhat
data.value: The aging report classifies amounts due to the organization (receivables) and due from it (payables) by age: under thirty days, thirty to sixty, sixty to ninety, or more. The older a receivable becomes, the higher the collection risk.

data.name: RepAgingHow
data.value:
1. Open the Reports menu and choose Aging.
2. Select the receivables type (customer receivables or supplier payables) and set the period.
3. Review the table and focus on the older buckets that need documented contact with the parties.
4. Export the report to build daily follow-up lists.

data.name: RepAgingConcept
data.value: The age of an amount is the difference between its due date and today. Older figures usually signal weak collection follow-up; the report also exposes recording errors, because an unexplained balance stands out clearly in an unreasonably old bucket.

data.name: RepCashFlowTitle
data.value: Cash Flows

data.name: RepCashFlowWhat
data.value: The cash flow report shows cash receipts and payments during the period, operating and investing, to reveal where liquidity came from and where it went. It complements the ratios because it observes the real movement of cash, not only the accounting direction.

data.name: RepCashFlowHow
data.value:
1. Open the Reports menu and choose Cash Flow.
2. Set the required period and generate the report.
3. Read the net operating and investing flows and compare them with the period's sales to confirm that cash received matches cash sales.
4. Export the report for your monthly liquidity review.

data.name: RepItemProfitabilityTitle
data.value: Item Profitability

data.name: RepItemProfitabilityWhat
data.value: The item profitability report calculates, for each item, what was sold, its margin, and its contribution, revealing which items build real profit and which consume effort without return, and steering pricing and purchasing decisions.

data.name: RepItemProfitabilityHow
data.value:
1. Open the Reports menu and choose Item Profitability.
2. Set the period and generate the report.
3. Sort the results by margin or contribution to surface the strongest and weakest items.
4. Compare periods to analyze the effect of price changes on sold quantities, then decide on documented data.

data.name: RepItemProfitabilityConcept
data.value: Margin is the sale price minus the unit cost; contribution is the unit profit multiplied by the quantity sold in the period. Fast-moving items with small margins can generate more profit than a high-margin item that sells slowly, which is why margin and contribution should be read together.

data.name: RepBudgetTitle
data.value: Estimated Budget

data.name: RepBudgetWhat
data.value: An estimated budget is a financial planning tool that sets expected targets for sales and expenses in the coming period so they can later be compared with actual performance. In this system it is built on the data available from sales and expense reports; it is not yet produced as a standalone report at this stage.

data.name: RepBudgetHow
data.value:
1. Estimate the coming months' sales from the seasonality, sales, and customer growth reports.
2. Estimate expenses from historical expense vouchers plus any expected increases.
3. Document the estimated figures and their basis so they become a reference point.
4. Compare planned versus actual monthly from the financial statements and adjust estimates against reality.

data.name: RepBudgetConcept
data.value: The essence of budgeting is not matching the estimate to the actual literally; the gap between them is what guides decisions: stop spending that exceeded the planned line, or increase purchasing of an item that beat its expected sales. A sound budget starts with realistic forecasts and is revised periodically.

data.name: SetUsersRolesTitle
data.value: Managing Users and Roles

data.name: SetUsersRolesWhat
data.value: The permissions module controls who logs into the system and what they see and do: users are people with login accounts, while roles carry specific permissions (such as POS, sales, or reports) and are assigned to users so each employee has exactly the permissions their job requires.

data.name: SetUsersRolesHow
data.value:
1. Open the Permissions menu from the top navigation and choose Roles.
2. Create a role, set its permissions, then assign users to it.
3. From the Users page add a new user with a name and a strong password and set their role, or edit an existing user's permissions.
4. Grant the least permissions each job needs, never share login accounts between employees, and review roles periodically as staff changes.

data.name: SetUsersRolesConcept
data.value: The least-privilege principle reduces errors and misuse: a cashier needs the POS but not invoice deletion, an accountant needs journal entries but not user management. Separating roles this way is organizational protection that stops permissions from quietly expanding.

data.name: SetSystemTitle
data.value: General System Settings

data.name: SetSystemWhat
data.value: The settings screen gathers the system-wide switches: enabling or disabling modules (such as POS and sales), and behavioral settings such as the POS grid limit and the electronic scale barcode behavior, plus other general preferences.

data.name: SetSystemHow
data.value:
1. Click the Settings button (the gear icon) at the top of the screen to open the page.
2. Enable or disable the module you want to show or hide from the menus.
3. Adjust the behavioral values according to company policy, then save.
4. The page may reload automatically after some changes to apply them.

data.name: SetSystemConcept
data.value: Settings are operating switches, not business records: changing them affects every user immediately and defines which modules appear and how they behave, so they are usually managed by the system administrator alone and are not changed in the middle of a working day without prior arrangement.

data.name: AccJournalEntriesConcept
data.value: The double-entry rule: every financial transaction has two equal sides, a debit and a credit. For example, a cash sale debits the cash account and credits the sales revenue account. If you total the effect of all entries, you will find that the value of assets equals liabilities plus equity; this is the heart of the accounting cycle.

data.name: AccFinancialStatementsConcept
data.value: The two statements are connected: the net profit shown in the income statement is added to equity in the balance sheet. This means any correction to earlier entries automatically changes the later statements, and the two should stay consistent at every month-end close.

data.name: InvUnitsConcept
data.value: Unit consistency is critical for accurate stock: recording 100 packs as 100 pieces corrupts the count and distorts costs. Stick to one clear base unit per item and keep it unchanged across screens, without parallel conversions the system does not support.

data.name: InvBatchesConcept
data.value: Each batch keeps its own cost, so the value of remaining units equals the total cost of their batches. When selling, units are priced from the soonest-expiring batch first, which makes inventory valuation and the value of spoilage more accurate than a single average for everything.

data.name: SalQuotesConcept
data.value: Keeping quotes separate from invoices protects stock: you can price any quantity without changing balances, and no stock movement or accounting entry occurs until the accepted quote is actually converted into an invoice.

data.name: PurBarcodeReceivingConcept
data.value: Barcode scanning is only a fast entry method; it runs through the same processing path as manual search and never bypasses the checks on quantity, cost, or batches. During rapid consecutive scans keep an eye on the last line, since scanner speeds can vary.

data.name: PosCashTransferConcept
data.value: A cash transfer does not change your total cash; it moves money between two cash accounts, so it does not affect shift results. Any undocumented shortage or surplus, by contrast, appears as a variance in the end-of-shift count, which is exactly when the system posts the cash-difference entry automatically.

data.name: PosShiftConcept
data.value: A positive variance is a shortage charged to the cash-differences account; a negative one is a surplus kept by the company. Posting the difference automatically keeps the books balanced and builds a permanent record of each cashier's discipline without manual handling.

data.name: ChkDueDatesConcept
data.value: Net monthly flow equals incoming checks due minus outgoing checks due. This number is a liquidity-planning tool: it lets the organization learn in advance that an upcoming month will have more outgoing obligations than incoming receipts, and act before a cash shortage hits.

data.name: HrLeavesConcept
data.value: Recording a leave is currently documentary in essence; if attendance and payroll are linked to these modules later, absent days will be calculated from the documented records retroactively, so accurate entry today prevents attendance disputes tomorrow.

data.name: RepCashFlowConcept
data.value: Accounting profit can look strong while the organization struggles with cash if sales are on credit; the cash flow report completes the picture with actual receipts and payments and reveals the gap that must be covered by financing or by tightening credit terms.
